contribution: The first chapter of the module introduces the quantisation of energy: the observations of the photoelectric effect that the wave model cannot explain, the photon energy $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, the electronvolt, the work function and Einstein's photoelectric equation $hf = W + E_\text{k,max}$ with its threshold frequencies, and the different roles of intensity and frequency.
learn: explain why the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by the wave model, and describe light as photons.
calculate the energy of a photon from its frequency or wavelength in joules and in electronvolts.
calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the released electrons and the threshold wavelength with the photoelectric equation.
prior: The speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave are related by the equation $v = f\lambda$ (chapter *How waves form and travel*)
The kinetic energy of a moving object is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ (chapter *Kinetic energy, potential energy and mechanical energy*)
Energy is conserved when it changes from one form to another (chapter *Forms of energy and conservation of energy*)

activities.text: A zinc plate is attached to an electroscope and charged negative, so the leaves of the electroscope are apart. When the teacher illuminates the plate in shielded apparatus with a small lamp that emits short-wavelength ultraviolet radiation (UV-C), the leaves drop within seconds: the plate loses electrons. When a bright red lamp that radiates many times more light power is placed in front of the same plate, the leaves stay apart even if the illumination continues for an hour.
activities.question: Why does weak UV-C radiation release electrons while strong red light does not, and what does this tell us about the energy of light?

activities.title: Review: frequency and wavelength
activities.prompt: Light always travels in a vacuum at the same speed $c$. The wavelength of violet light is about $400\,\text{nm}$ and that of red light about $650\,\text{nm}$. Which light has the greater frequency?

choices.text: Violet, because a shorter wavelength means a greater frequency.
choices.feedback: Correct. The basic equation of wave motion $c = f\lambda$ gives $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$ (chapter *How waves form and travel*), so a shorter wavelength gives a greater frequency. The frequency of violet light is about $7.5 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ and that of red light about $4.6 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

choices.text: Red, because a longer wave oscillates more often.
choices.feedback: When the speed of the wave is the same, a longer wave has time to oscillate *less often* per second: $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$. The frequency of red light is therefore smaller than that of violet light.

choices.text: The frequencies are equal, because both travel at the speed of light.
choices.feedback: The same speed does not mean the same frequency. In the equation $c = f\lambda$ the speed is the same, so the product of wavelength and frequency is the same: a shorter wavelength means a greater frequency.

activities.title: Prediction 1: brighter red light
activities.prompt: A sodium plate is illuminated with red light of wavelength $650\,\text{nm}$. No electrons are released. What happens when the intensity of the same light is increased many times?

choices.text: Electrons start to be released when the light is bright enough, because more energy arrives at the plate each second.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: at a wavelength of $650\,\text{nm}$ the number of released electrons is $0$ at any intensity. Brighter light does bring more energy, but it comes as more photons, each of which has an energy of only $1.91\,\text{eV}$. That is not enough for the work function of sodium, $2.28\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: No electrons are released at any intensity, because the colour of the light decides whether electrons are released.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: at a wavelength of $650\,\text{nm}$ no electrons at all are released, even at an intensity of $100\,\%$. The energy of one photon is $1.91\,\text{eV}$, which is smaller than the work function of sodium, $2.28\,\text{eV}$. The intensity changes only the number of photons.

choices.text: Electrons start to be released after a while, when they have had time to collect enough energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: no electrons are released even if the illumination continues. An electron does not collect energy from many photons but receives the energy of one photon at once, $1.91\,\text{eV}$, which is not enough for the work function $2.28\,\text{eV}$.

activities.title: Prediction 2: double intensity
activities.prompt: A sodium plate is illuminated with violet light of wavelength $405\,\text{nm}$, and electrons are released. The intensity of the light is doubled. What happens to the released electrons?

choices.text: Twice as many electrons are released, and the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons doubles.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute part of this: the number of electrons doubles, but the maximum kinetic energy stays at $0.78\,\text{eV}$. One electron always receives the energy of one photon, and the photon energy depends only on the wavelength.

choices.text: Twice as many electrons are released, but the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons stays the same.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: at an intensity of $20\,\%$ the figure shows $8$ electrons released per second and at $40\,\%$ $16$, but the maximum kinetic energy is $0.78\,\text{eV}$ every time. Brighter light brings more photons of the same kind.

choices.text: The same number of electrons is released, but they are faster, because brighter light brings more energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the maximum kinetic energy stays at $0.78\,\text{eV}$, and twice as many electrons are released. The extra energy comes as more photons, each of which releases at most one electron.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the colour of the light is the same.
choices.feedback: The colour, that is the wavelength, determines the energy of one photon, so the maximum kinetic energy indeed does not change. In the values of the model, however, the number of electrons doubles, because twice as many photons arrive each second.

activities.text: Illuminate a metal plate with different wavelengths and intensities. Observe whether electrons are released, how many, and with how much energy.
activities.howto: Energies are in electronvolts ($\text{eV}$). It is a convenient unit for the small energies of photons and electrons: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Adjust the wavelength $\lambda$ and the intensity of the light and choose the metal. The lamp sends photons as wavy arrows whose colour is the colour of the light; ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see, is drawn in violet. The blue dots are released electrons. On the right (below on a phone) the energies are to scale: the left bar is the energy of one photon $hf$, the right one is the work function $W$ of the electron, and on top of it is the maximum kinetic energy $E_\text{k,max}$. The readouts show the frequency, the photon energy, the work function, the maximum kinetic energy and the number of electrons released per second in the picture. *Speed* changes only the pace of the motion in the picture, not the readouts.
activities.model: Light arrives as photons whose energy is $E = hf$. One photon gives all of its energy to one electron; the electron does not collect energy from several photons. In the model every photon with enough energy releases an electron, but in reality only a small fraction of the photons release an electron, and far more electrons are released, by a factor of billions, than in the picture. The kinetic energies of the released electrons vary, because some lose energy on their way to the surface of the metal; the readout shows the maximum. The work functions are typical table values: the cleanliness of a real surface changes them. The intensity of the model is the number of photons per second; in real light of the same power there are fewer photons at a short wavelength, because each photon carries more energy. The readouts are values calculated by the model. The results of the model correspond to what was measured in the experiments of the early 1900s.
activities.calc: The frequency of a photon is $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$ and its energy is $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, where $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$ and $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$. The energy in electronvolts is obtained by dividing by $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{eV}}$. If $E \geq W$, the maximum kinetic energy is $E_\text{k,max} = E - W$, otherwise no electrons are released. In the picture $0.4$ photons arrive per second for each percentage point of intensity, so at an intensity of $50\,\%$ there are $20$ per second.

activities.title: Experiment 1: red light, only the intensity changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. A sodium plate is illuminated with red light, $\lambda = 650\,\text{nm}$; change only the intensity. Record the readouts at at least two intensities, for example $20\,\%$ and $100\,\%$. Are electrons released at any intensity?

activities.title: Experiment 2: violet light, only the intensity changes
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. A sodium plate is illuminated with violet light, $\lambda = 405\,\text{nm}$; change only the intensity. Record the readouts at least at the intensities $20\,\%$ and $40\,\%$, preferably also $100\,\%$. How do the number of electrons and the maximum kinetic energy change?

activities.title: Experiment 3: only the wavelength changes
activities.intro: First guess: does the maximum kinetic energy increase or decrease when the wavelength gets shorter, that is when the frequency increases? The intensity is now $50\,\%$, so in the model the same number of photons arrives each second at every wavelength; change only the wavelength. Record the readouts at at least the wavelengths $300\,\text{nm}$, $400\,\text{nm}$ and $500\,\text{nm}$. Then find the wavelength at which the release of electrons stops, and record the readouts on both sides of it. Compare how much the photon energy and the maximum kinetic energy change between the measurements.

question.prompt: Read from your table the longest wavelength at which electrons are still released from sodium. Check the estimate by calculating it from the work function of sodium, $W = 2.28\,\text{eV}$ (use $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$). Give the answer in nanometres.
hints: Electrons are just barely released when the energy of one photon is equal to the work function.
Solve the wavelength $\lambda_0$ from the equation $\tfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = W$. Convert $W$ to joules first.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated the threshold frequency $f_0 = \tfrac{W}{h}$. The question asks for the wavelength: $\lambda_0 = \tfrac{c}{f_0}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** work function of sodium $W = 2.28\,\text{eV}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$; from the table: at a wavelength of $540\,\text{nm}$ electrons are released, at $545\,\text{nm}$ they are not

**Find:** the longest wavelength that releases electrons, that is the threshold wavelength $\lambda_0$, in nanometres

**Principle:** One photon gives its energy to one electron, so an electron is just barely released when the photon energy is exactly equal to the work function. At longer wavelengths the photon energy is smaller than $W$.

**Reading the table:** In the table the maximum kinetic energy decreases as the wavelength grows, and at $540\,\text{nm}$ it is only about $0.02\,\text{eV}$; at $545\,\text{nm}$ no electrons are released. The limit is therefore between these, at about $544\,\text{nm}$.

**Formula:** $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = W$, so $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W}$

**Conversions:** $W = 2.28\,\text{eV} = 2.28 \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 3.653 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$; the result from metres to nanometres, $1\,\text{m} = 10^{9}\,\text{nm}$

**Substitution:** The numerator is $hc = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s} = 1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}$, so $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}}{3.653 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 5.439 \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 543.9\,\text{nm}$

**Answer:** $544\,\text{nm}$, three significant figures like the work function $2.28\,\text{eV}$.

**Reasonableness:** The calculated value is between the table limits $540\,\text{nm}$ and $545\,\text{nm}$. With round numbers $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 2.28\,\text{eV} \approx 544\,\text{nm}$. This is green light, so red and yellow light do not release electrons from sodium, as was seen with red light in experiment 1.

activities.title: Conclusion: what decides the release?
activities.prompt: On the basis of your tables, write: what did the intensity change and what did it not change? How did the maximum kinetic energy change with the photon energy? Why did red light not release electrons from sodium at any intensity?
activities.model: With red light, $650\,\text{nm}$, no electrons were released at any intensity: the photon energy was $1.91\,\text{eV}$ every time, smaller than the work function of sodium, $2.28\,\text{eV}$. With violet light, doubling the intensity doubled the number of electrons, for example from $8$ to $16$ per second, but the maximum kinetic energy stayed at $0.78\,\text{eV}$. When the wavelength got shorter from $500\,\text{nm}$ to $400\,\text{nm}$, the photon energy grew from $2.48\,\text{eV}$ to $3.10\,\text{eV}$ and the maximum kinetic energy by the same amount, from $0.20\,\text{eV}$ to $0.82\,\text{eV}$; the difference $W = 2.28\,\text{eV}$ stayed the same. The release stopped at about $544\,\text{nm}$. Explanation: one photon gives its energy to one electron, so the photon energy decides whether an electron is released and how great its kinetic energy can be, and the intensity decides only the number of photons and therefore of electrons. The values are calculated by the model.
criteria: I said that red light did not release electrons at any intensity, because the photon energy was smaller than the work function.
I said that the intensity changed the number of electrons but not the maximum kinetic energy, and I gave numbers from the table.
I said that the maximum kinetic energy grew by as much as the photon energy, that is $E_\text{k,max} = hf - W$.
I explained the observations by one photon giving its energy to one electron.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model in the experiments and with the equation $hf = W + E_\text{k,max}$. Then return to the opening question: why does weak UV-C radiation discharge a zinc plate while bright red light does not?

activities.title: Find the mistake
activities.prompt:
A student calculates the energy of a photon of green light when the wavelength is $500\,\text{nm}$. She writes

$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s} : 500 = 3.97 \cdot 10^{-28}\,\text{J}$

Where is the mistake?

choices.text: The wavelength has not been converted to metres: $500\,\text{nm} = 500 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$, so the correct result is $3.97 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. When the denominator is just the number $500$, the units do not cancel to joules, and the result is a billion times too small. The error could also have been noticed from the order of magnitude: the energy of a photon of visible light is about $10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, that is a few electronvolts.

choices.text: The formula is wrong: the photon energy is $E = h\lambda$, because the energy grows with the wavelength.
choices.feedback: The photon energy is $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$: it *decreases* as the wavelength grows. This is why photons of red light have less energy than those of violet light. The error in the calculation is in the unit: $500\,\text{nm}$ is $500 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$.

choices.text: The Planck constant is wrong: it should be $6.626 \cdot 10^{34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$.
choices.feedback: The Planck constant is $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, a very small number, because the energy of a single photon is small. The mistake is that the wavelength has not been converted to metres.

choices.text: There is no mistake in the calculation; photons are so small that their energy is of this order of magnitude.
choices.feedback: The energy of a photon of visible light is about $3 \cdot 10^{-19}$–$5 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, not $10^{-28}\,\text{J}$. In the calculation the wavelength has been left in nanometres, although $h$ and $c$ contain the metre: $500\,\text{nm} = 500 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A photomultiplier tube detects very weak light: the light releases electrons from its cathode, and the tube amplifies their current so that it can be measured. The work function of the cathode of one tube is $1.90\,\text{eV}$. What is the longest wavelength of light that the tube can detect? Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Give the answer in nanometres.
hints: The tube detects light only if one photon can release an electron. What condition for the photon energy follows from this?
At the longest detectable wavelength the photon energy is exactly the work function: $\tfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = W$.
$W = 1.90 \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 3.044 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, and $\lambda_0 = \tfrac{hc}{W}$. Finally convert metres to nanometres.

mistakes.feedback: This is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \tfrac{W}{h}$ in hertz. The question asks for the wavelength: $\lambda_0 = \tfrac{c}{f_0} = \tfrac{hc}{W}$.

You left the work function in electronvolts. The Planck constant is in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$, so $W$ must also be converted to joules: $1.90\,\text{eV} = 1.90 \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** work function of the cathode $W = 1.90\,\text{eV}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

**Find:** the longest detectable wavelength, that is the threshold wavelength $\lambda_0$, in nanometres

**Principle:** The tube detects light only when the light releases electrons from the cathode (the photoelectric effect). One photon gives its energy to one electron, so the photon energy must be at least equal to the work function. The weakness of the light is no problem, because already one photon with enough energy releases an electron; at long wavelengths the photon energy is not enough.

**Formula:** $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = W$, so $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W}$

**Conversions:** $W = 1.90\,\text{eV} = 1.90 \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 3.044 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$; the result from metres to nanometres, $1\,\text{m} = 10^{9}\,\text{nm}$

**Substitution:** $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{3.044 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 6.526 \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 652.6\,\text{nm}$

**Answer:** $653\,\text{nm}$, three significant figures like the work function $1.90\,\text{eV}$.

**Reasonableness:** With round numbers $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 1.90\,\text{eV} \approx 653\,\text{nm}$. The work function is smaller than that of sodium, $2.28\,\text{eV}$, so the threshold wavelength must be longer than that of sodium, $544\,\text{nm}$, and red light starts at about $620\,\text{nm}$, so the tube detects the visible light up to the beginning of the red end; deep red, such as $700\,\text{nm}$, it does not detect.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. The tasks of level 1 use one formula, the tasks of level 2 combine two steps, such as the photon energy and the work function, and level 3 requires reasoning in a new situation.

activities.title: 1. Which lamp?
activities.prompt: The work function of zinc is $4.31\,\text{eV}$. Available are a $1\,\text{W}$ UV-C lamp, $\lambda = 254\,\text{nm}$, whose photon energy is $4.88\,\text{eV}$, and a $100\,\text{W}$ red lamp, $\lambda = 650\,\text{nm}$, whose photon energy is $1.91\,\text{eV}$. Which one releases electrons from a zinc plate?

choices.text: Only the UV-C lamp, because one of its photons is enough to release an electron.
choices.feedback: Correct. The photon energy $4.88\,\text{eV}$ is greater than the work function $4.31\,\text{eV}$. The photons of the red lamp, $1.91\,\text{eV}$, are not enough, even though far more of them arrive.

choices.text: Only the red lamp, because its power is a hundred times greater.
choices.feedback: Power tells how much energy the lamp emits per second. Many red photons arrive, but none of them is enough: one electron receives the energy of one photon, and the $1.91\,\text{eV}$ of red light remains smaller than the work function $4.31\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: Both, but the red lamp releases more electrons, because its power is greater.
choices.feedback: The red lamp releases no electrons at all: its photon energy $1.91\,\text{eV}$ is smaller than the work function. Energy does not accumulate from several photons to one electron.

choices.text: Neither, because $1\,\text{W}$ is too small a power and the frequency of red light is too low.
choices.feedback: A small power means few photons, but every UV-C photon, $4.88\,\text{eV}$, is enough on its own to release an electron. With the UV-C lamp fewer electrons are therefore released than with a high-power UV lamp, but some are released.

activities.title: 2. A photon from a blue LED
activities.prompt: A blue LED emits light with a wavelength of $450\,\text{nm}$. What is the energy of one photon? Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Give the answer in electronvolts.
hints: The photon energy depends on the frequency, and the frequency is obtained from the wavelength.
Substitute $h$, $c$ and $\lambda = 450 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$, which gives $E = 4.414 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Convert this to electronvolts.

mistakes.feedback: This is the energy in joules. Convert it to electronvolts by dividing by $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{eV}}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** wavelength $\lambda = 450\,\text{nm}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

**Find:** the energy $E$ of one photon in electronvolts

**Principle:** The energy of light is quantised into photons, and the energy of one photon is $E = hf$. The light of an LED has almost a single wavelength, so all photons have about the same energy. The frequency is obtained from the wavelength: $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$.

**Formula:** $E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$

**Conversions:** $\lambda = 450\,\text{nm} = 450 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$; the energy from joules to electronvolts by dividing by $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{eV}}$

**Substitution:** $E = \dfrac{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{450 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 4.414 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = \dfrac{4.414 \cdot 10^{-19}}{1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}}\,\text{eV} = 2.756\,\text{eV}$

**Answer:** $2.76\,\text{eV}$, three significant figures like the wavelength $450\,\text{nm}$.

**Reasonableness:** With round numbers $1240\,\text{eV}\,\text{nm} : 450\,\text{nm} \approx 2.8\,\text{eV}$. Blue is at the short-wavelength end of visible light, so its photon energy is close to the upper end of the range $1.8$–$3.1\,\text{eV}$.

activities.title: 3. Explain: brighter light
activities.prompt: A friend says: “If blue light is made brighter, the released electrons fly faster, because the light brings more energy.” Evaluate the claim. Explain with the photon model what increasing the intensity changes and what it does not.
criteria: I say that brighter light brings more photons each second, but the energy $hf$ of each photon stays the same.
I explain that one electron receives the energy of one photon, so the maximum kinetic energy $hf - W$ does not change.
I conclude that the intensity increases the number of released electrons, not their maximum speed.
I say that faster electrons are obtained with a shorter wavelength, that is a higher frequency.
activities.model: The claim does not hold. Brighter light does bring more energy per second, but it comes as more photons, each of which still has the energy $hf$, because the colour of the light, that is its frequency, does not change. One photon gives its energy to one electron, so the maximum kinetic energy of an electron is always $E_\text{k,max} = hf - W$ and does not depend on the intensity. Brighter light therefore releases more electrons per second, and the current they form grows, but the fastest electrons fly as fast as before. Faster electrons are obtained only with a higher frequency, for example with violet or ultraviolet light.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first on your own and open the answer only after that.
